nagar.t: Nagar, a major city of the northern Syrian plains at Tell Brak, famed in the 3rd millennium BCE for breeding prized draught equids and later seized by Akkad.
nagar.o: Tell Brak in the Khabur basin had been one of the largest settlements of northern Mesopotamia since the 4th millennium BCE. By c. 2600 BCE it was the centre of a kingdom called Nagar, which appears in the Ebla archives as a regional power on the route between Syria and the Tigris.
nagar.r: Ebla texts show Nagar exchanging gifts, envoys and royal marriages with its western neighbour, and supplying expensive kunga, hybrid draught animals bred from donkeys and wild asses, used to pull royal vehicles. Little is known of its internal government, since few texts have been found at the site itself.
nagar.e: Around 2300 BCE the Akkadian Empire took control; Naram-Sin built a massive fortified storehouse at Tell Brak. After Akkad's collapse a Hurrian kingdom called Nawar ruled from the city, and Tell Brak stayed occupied into the 2nd millennium BCE.

niya.t: Niya, a small kingdom of the middle Orontes, known for the elephant herds that pharaoh Thutmose III hunted in its marshes.
niya.o: Niya lay in the middle Orontes valley, probably near Apamea, in a region of marshes and fertile land. It emerged in the 15th century BCE as a minor kingdom in the orbit of the Mitanni Empire.
niya.r: Little is known of its government. Thutmose III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom recorded hunting about 120 elephants there, and the city appears in the Amarna letters and the archives of Alalakh. Its king Takuwa visited Egypt to pledge loyalty.
niya.e: Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire took Niya c. 1340 BCE during his conquest of Syria, and it disappears as a kingdom.

nurmekund.t: Small Estonian district in the centre of the country, mentioned in Henry of Livonia's chronicle and conquered in the 1220s.
nurmekund.o: Nurmekund, called Normegunde in the sources, was a minor Estonian land in central Estonia, between Sakala, Järvamaa and Alempois. It is known only from brief mentions in the chronicle of the Livonian crusade.
nurmekund.r: It was probably a union of a few parishes under elders, sharing the customs and pagan religion of the larger Estonian counties around it. No leaders or details of its organisation are recorded.
nurmekund.e: Nurmekund was subdued during the conquest of Estonia, completed in 1224, and passed to the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and later the Livonian Order.

northern-ireland.t: The part of the United Kingdom in north-east Ireland, created by partition in 1921 and marked by decades of conflict and a power-sharing peace.
northern-ireland.o: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 created Northern Ireland from six of Ulster's nine counties, where Protestants, mostly unionists, were a majority. Its Parliament opened in June 1921, and it opted out of the Irish Free State in December 1922.
northern-ireland.r: Northern Ireland was governed for fifty years by the Ulster Unionist Party from Stormont, with discrimination against the Catholic, mainly nationalist minority. Belfast was a centre of shipbuilding and linen. The civil rights movement of the late 1960s was followed by the Troubles, which killed about 3,600 people, and direct rule from London from 1972.
northern-ireland.e: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 established a power-sharing Assembly and Executive and confirmed that Northern Ireland remains in the United Kingdom unless its people vote otherwise.

neo-inca-state.t: The last independent Inca state, which held out in the forested mountains of Vilcabamba for 35 years after the Spanish conquest of Cusco.
neo-inca-state.o: In 1536 the Inca ruler Manco Inca, installed by the Spanish as a puppet, rebelled and besieged Cusco for months. After failing to retake the city, he withdrew in 1537 to Vitcos and then Vilcabamba, a remote region in the montane forest northwest of Cusco, where he founded a new Inca state.
neo-inca-state.r: From Vilcabamba, Manco Inca waged guerrilla war against the Spanish and kept up Inca rituals and court life. After his murder in 1544 by Spanish refugees, his sons ruled in turn. Sayri Túpac accepted Spanish terms and left in 1558. Titu Cusi Yupanqui negotiated with the Spanish, allowed missionaries and dictated an account of the conquest, the Instrucción, in 1570.
neo-inca-state.e: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo sent an expedition in 1572 that captured the last ruler, Túpac Amaru, who was executed in Cusco. Vilcabamba was abandoned and forgotten until explorers, including Hiram Bingham in 1911, rediscovered its ruins at Espíritu Pampa.

naxos-sicily.t: The first Greek colony in Sicily, founded by Chalcidians in 734 BCE beneath Mount Etna and destroyed by Dionysius I in 403 BCE.
naxos-sicily.o: According to Thucydides, Chalcidians from Euboea, joined by Naxians from the Aegean, founded Naxos in 734 BCE on the Schisò headland below modern Taormina, led by Theocles. As the first landfall for ships crossing from Greece, it became the starting point for Greek colonisation of the island.
naxos-sicily.r: Naxos was small but symbolically important: its altar of Apollo Archegetes, 'the Founder', was where envoys sailing from Sicily to Greece made sacrifice. Within a few years it sent out settlers to found Leontini and Catana. It grew vines on the slopes of Etna, and its coins with Dionysus and a satyr are celebrated. Hippocrates of Gela subdued it around 495 BCE, and later it was often allied with Athens and Leontini against Syracuse.
naxos-sicily.e: Dionysius I captured Naxos by treachery in 403 BCE, sold its people into slavery and gave its land to the Sicels. In 358 BCE survivors and Sicels founded Tauromenium on the hill above. Excavations at Giardini Naxos have revealed the walls, sanctuaries and street grid.

cr.a: Alun Salt from Derby and Leicester, UK

neustria.t: Western kingdom of the Merovingian Franks, centred on Paris and Soissons, and the long rival of Austrasia.
neustria.o: Neustria, the new western land, took shape after the division of 561, when Chilperic I received Soissons and the lands between the Loire and the Scheldt. It later included Paris, Rouen and Tours.
neustria.r: Chilperic and his queen Fredegund waged a bitter feud with Austrasia's Sigebert I and Brunhild. Their son Chlothar II reunited the Frankish kingdoms in 613. Neustria had a strongly Gallo-Roman population and rich abbeys such as Saint-Denis, and in the 7th century its mayor Ebroin dominated politics.
neustria.e: The Austrasian Pippin of Herstal defeated the Neustrians at Tertry in 687, and Charles Martel finally crushed the Neustrian mayor Ragenfrid in 717 to 719. After 751 Neustria became a region of the Carolingian realm, and the name was later applied to the land between the Seine and the Loire.

novgorod-republic.t: Lord Novgorod the Great, a merchant republic of the Russian north that hired and fired its princes and traded furs with the Hanseatic League.
novgorod-republic.o: Novgorod on the Volkhov had long been the second city of Kievan Rus', usually governed by a son of the Kievan prince. In 1136 its citizens expelled Prince Vsevolod Mstislavich, and from then on they chose their own princes under contract, limiting them to military command. Historians date the republic from this event.
novgorod-republic.r: Power lay with the town assembly, the veche, the elected posadnik and tysyatsky, the boyar families and the archbishop. Novgorod controlled a huge northern hinterland reaching to the White Sea and the Urals, exporting furs, wax and walrus ivory to the Hanseatic merchants of the Peterhof. Hundreds of birchbark letters show widespread literacy. Its prince Alexander Nevsky defeated the Swedes in 1240 and the Teutonic Knights in 1242.
novgorod-republic.e: Novgorod sought Lithuanian help against the Grand Duchy of Moscow, a party led by the boyar widow Marfa Boretskaya. Ivan III crushed its army at the Shelon in 1471, annexed the city in 1478 and carried off the veche bell. Its leading families were deported and the Hanseatic office was closed in 1494.
novgorod-republic.la: Old Novgorod dialect of Old East Slavic

novantae.t: People of Galloway in south-west Scotland, named by Ptolemy, whose peninsula and towns faced the Irish Sea.
novantae.o: Ptolemy lists the Novantae in south-western Scotland, giving their name to a peninsula, the Novantarum Promontorium, usually identified with the Rhins of Galloway, and naming two towns, Locopibia and Rerigonium. They grew from Iron Age communities living in duns, crannogs and small forts along the coast and inland valleys of Galloway.
novantae.r: No rulers or written records survive. Agricola's campaigns of about 81 probably brought Roman troops into Galloway, and forts were built at Glenlochar and Gatehouse of Fleet. Their position on the Irish Sea gave them close contact with Ireland and the Isle of Man, and their society was rural and pastoral.
novantae.e: Roman control of the region was brief, and the Novantae disappear from the written record after Ptolemy. Their territory later formed part of British kingdoms of the north, possibly Rheged, before Northumbrian expansion into Galloway in the 7th and 8th centuries.

nadruvians.t: Prussian people of Nadruvia, between the Pregolya and Neman rivers, among the last to be conquered by the Teutonic Knights.
nadruvians.o: Nadruvia lay in the north-east of Prussia, south of the Neman, in what is now the Kaliningrad region. Its people were Prussians, known mainly from Peter of Dusburg's chronicle, which describes a sacred site called Romowe somewhere in the territory, though its existence is debated.
nadruvians.r: They lived from farming, cattle and forest resources, under local nobles with hillforts. Their land bordered Scalovia and Sudovia and was close to Lithuania.
nadruvians.e: After defeating the Great Prussian Uprising, the Teutonic Order conquered Nadruvia in 1274-1277. Much of the population fled or was resettled, and the region became a thinly peopled frontier of the Order's state, later repopulated by Lithuanians and Germans.

north-german-confederation.t: Prussian-led federal state formed after the defeat of Austria in 1866, the direct forerunner of the German Empire.
north-german-confederation.o: Prussia's victory in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 dissolved the German Confederation. Prussia annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau and Frankfurt and joined the remaining states north of the Main in a new federation. Its constitution, drafted largely by Otto von Bismarck, came into force on 1 July 1867.
north-german-confederation.r: The King of Prussia held the federal presidency and commanded the armies, and Bismarck was federal chancellor. A Federal Council represented the governments, and a Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage. The confederation unified weights, coinage, trade law and criminal law, and the south German states were tied to it by military alliances and the customs union.
north-german-confederation.e: During the Franco-Prussian War, Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse joined in 1870. The confederation was renamed the German Empire, and William I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles on 18 January 1871.

neutral-moresnet.t: A tiny wedge-shaped territory between Belgium and Prussia, left jointly governed for a century because neither side would give up its zinc mine.
neutral-moresnet.o: After 1815, the Netherlands and Prussia could not agree on the border near Aachen because both wanted the valuable Vieille Montagne zinc mine at Kelmis. In 1816 they left a small triangle of land under joint administration, with Belgium taking the Dutch role after 1830.
neutral-moresnet.r: Neutral Moresnet was run by a mayor and two royal commissioners, one from each neighbour. Its residents paid low taxes and avoided conscription, and the Vieille Montagne company dominated the economy. After the mine was exhausted in 1885, enthusiasts promoted it as a possible Esperanto state called Amikejo, and the territory became known for its gambling and distillery.
neutral-moresnet.e: The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 assigned the territory to the Kingdom of Belgium, effective in 1920. Kelmis, its main village, is now part of Belgium's German-speaking community.

natangians.t: Prussian people of Natangia whose leader Herkus Monte led the Great Prussian Uprising against the Teutonic Order from 1260.
natangians.o: Natangia lay south of the Pregolya river in central Prussia, divided today between Russia's Kaliningrad region and Poland. Its people were Prussians organised in districts under nobles, known from Peter of Dusburg's chronicle.
natangians.r: The Natangians farmed fertile land and defended themselves from hillforts. The Teutonic Order first subdued them around 1240, but they kept their nobility and pagan beliefs under thin Christian rule. Herkus Monte, a Natangian noble educated in Magdeburg, became the most famous Prussian leader.
natangians.e: After the Order's defeat at Durbe in 1260, Herkus Monte led the Great Prussian Uprising, winning at Pokarwis in 1261. He was captured and hanged in 1273, and by 1274 the Natangians were defeated. Natangia became part of the Order's state and, later, of Ducal Prussia.

nuhashshe.t: Nuhashshe, a group of small Syrian kingdoms between the Orontes and the Euphrates, fought over by Mitanni, Egypt and the Hittites.
nuhashshe.o: The lands of Nuhashshe lay in the steppe and farmland south of Aleppo. In the 15th century BCE their rulers were vassals of the Mitanni Empire, and the region appears in Egyptian records of campaigns by Thutmose III and in the Amarna letters.
nuhashshe.r: Nuhashshe was a cluster of local kingdoms rather than a single state, with a leading king who represented the region in treaties. Its rulers moved between Egyptian, Mitannian and Hittite loyalties as each power advanced.
nuhashshe.e: Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire conquered the region in the 14th century BCE and made its king a vassal by treaty. Rebellions under Mursili II were suppressed, and the region later reappeared as Lu'ash.

nitiobroges.t: Gallic people of the middle Garonne around Agen, whose king Teutomatus fought for Vercingetorix at Gergovia.
nitiobroges.o: The Nitiobroges lived on the Garonne around Aginnum (Agen), at the border between the Celtic peoples and the Aquitani. Caesar notes that their king Ollovico had been honoured by the Roman Senate as a friend.
nitiobroges.r: They were ruled by kings in Caesar's day. Their land lay on the river route from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, and their coins circulated widely in south-western Gaul.
nitiobroges.e: Ollovico's son Teutomatus joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE with cavalry raised in Aquitania; during the attack on Gergovia he escaped from his tent half-dressed on a wounded horse. Under Rome Aginnum became a civitas capital, the origin of Agen.

nizari-ismailis-of-syria.t: The Syrian branch of the Nizari Ismailis, the 'Assassins' of Crusader legend, who ruled a network of mountain castles around Masyaf.
nizari-ismailis-of-syria.o: Nizari missionaries sent from Alamut in Iran first worked in Aleppo and Damascus but were driven out by massacres. From 1132 they acquired castles in the Jabal Bahra, the coastal mountains of Syria, including Qadmus, Kahf and in 1140-1141 Masyaf.
nizari-ismailis-of-syria.r: The castles formed a small state led by a chief missionary appointed from Alamut. Rashid al-Din Sinan, the original Old Man of the Mountain, led it from about 1162 to 1193, making it largely independent. The Nizaris used targeted killings by devotees against powerful enemies, including Conrad of Montferrat in 1192, and twice attempted to kill Saladin. They also paid tribute to the Hospitallers at times.
nizari-ismailis-of-syria.e: After the Mongols destroyed Alamut in 1256, the Syrian castles survived, but the Mamluk sultan Baybars took them one by one between 1270 and 1273. The Nizari community remained in the region, notably around Salamiyah and Masyaf.

neapolis.t: Greek 'new city' on the Bay of Naples, founded from Cumae, which kept its Greek speech and customs long after becoming Rome's ally in 326 BCE.
neapolis.o: Cumae founded Neapolis around 470 BCE beside an older settlement, Parthenope, named after a Siren whose tomb was shown there and which became known as Palaepolis, 'old city'. The new town was laid out on a regular grid whose main streets still shape central Naples.
neapolis.r: Neapolis grew through trade and gained importance after Cumae fell to the Campanians around 421 BCE. Athenian settlers are said to have joined it in the 5th century BCE, and it later admitted Campanian families to citizenship. Its coins with a man-headed bull and its torch race in honour of Parthenope are well known. It remained a centre of Greek culture in Campania.
neapolis.e: After a Roman siege in 327–326 BCE, the city made a treaty with Rome on favourable terms and became a loyal naval ally. It kept Greek language and institutions into the Empire, attracting Roman writers such as Virgil, and grew into Naples.

nervii.t: The fiercest of the Belgic peoples, who banned wine and luxuries and almost defeated Caesar at the Battle of the Sabis in 57 BCE.
nervii.o: The Nervii lived in the Hainaut region of modern Belgium and northern France, between the Scheldt and the Sambre. Caesar reports that they forbade merchants and wine, believing luxuries weakened courage, and that they were proud of their Germanic descent.
nervii.r: They had no cavalry to speak of and fought on foot, using thick hedges of bent saplings to block their land against raiders. Their war leader in 57 BCE was Boduognatus.
nervii.e: At the Sabis (probably the Sambre) in 57 BCE they surprised Caesar's camp and were crushed only after a desperate battle. In 54 BCE they besieged Quintus Cicero's winter camp. Under Rome their chief town was Bagacum (Bavay), later Cambrai.

najdiyya.t: A Kharijite state in central and eastern Arabia that briefly ruled al-Yamama, Bahrain and Oman during the civil war of the 680s.
najdiyya.o: The Najdiyya took their name from Najda ibn Amir al-Hanafi, a Kharijite leader who broke with the more extreme Azariqa. During the Second Fitna he seized al-Yamama, his tribe's homeland in Najd, around 686 and was acknowledged as commander of the faithful by his followers.
najdiyya.r: Najda's forces conquered Bahrain, Oman and parts of Yemen and Hadramawt and threatened Ta'if, challenging the Caliphate of Ibn al-Zubayr. He was more moderate than other Kharijites, allowing those who did not join him to live unharmed and relying on reasoned judgement where the Quran was silent. Internal disputes over the treatment of captives and payments to followers divided the movement.
najdiyya.e: Around 691 his own followers deposed and killed Najda and turned to Abu Fudayk. After the Umayyads reunited the caliphate, an army sent by Abd al-Malik defeated Abu Fudayk in Bahrain in 693, ending the state.

north-sea-empire.t: The short-lived union of England, Denmark and Norway under Cnut the Great, which made the North Sea the centre of an Anglo-Scandinavian realm.
north-sea-empire.o: Cnut, son of the Danish king Sweyn Forkbeard, conquered England in 1016 after the death of Edmund Ironside. He inherited Denmark from his brother Harald around 1018 and, after driving out Olaf Haraldsson, took Norway in 1028, also claiming lordship over part of the Swedes.
north-sea-empire.r: Cnut ruled mainly from England, often from Winchester, keeping English institutions, issuing law codes and marrying Emma of Normandy, widow of Æthelred the Unready. He governed Denmark and Norway through regents, including his son Harthacnut and the earls of Lade. A pilgrimage to Rome in 1027, where he attended Conrad II's coronation, raised his standing among Christian rulers.
north-sea-empire.e: Cnut died at Shaftesbury in 1035, and his realm broke apart. Norway rejected Danish rule under Magnus the Good, while his sons Harold Harefoot and Harthacnut divided England and Denmark. After Harthacnut's death in 1042 the English throne returned to Edward the Confessor, and the Kingdom of Denmark and the Kingdom of Norway went their own ways.

nazi-germany.t: Hitler's totalitarian dictatorship, which launched the Second World War and carried out the Holocaust before its total defeat in 1945.
nazi-germany.o: Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933. Using the Reichstag fire decree and the Enabling Act of March 1933, the Nazis abolished civil liberties, banned other parties, dissolved trade unions and subordinated the German states. On Hindenburg's death in 1934 Hitler combined the offices of chancellor and president as Führer.
nazi-germany.r: The regime ruled through terror, propaganda and the SS and Gestapo, and persecuted Jews through the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and the November pogrom of 1938. It rearmed, annexed Austria and the Sudetenland in 1938 and invaded Poland in 1939, starting the Second World War. In occupied Europe it murdered some six million Jews, as well as Roma, Soviet prisoners and others.
nazi-germany.e: Allied armies invaded Germany from east and west, Hitler killed himself in Berlin on 30 April 1945, and the Wehrmacht surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945. Germany was occupied and divided, and its leaders were tried at Nuremberg.

norse-greenland.t: Europe's most remote medieval society, the Norse farming settlements in south-west Greenland that lasted almost five centuries and then vanished.
norse-greenland.o: Erik the Red, outlawed from Iceland, led settlers to Greenland around 985, founding the Eastern Settlement near modern Qaqortoq and a smaller Western Settlement near Nuuk. His son Leif Erikson sailed from Greenland to North America around 1000 and is credited with bringing Christianity.
norse-greenland.r: The colonists raised cattle, sheep and goats and hunted seals and caribou. Their key export was walrus ivory, sent to Europe through Norway. They held their own assembly, and from 1126 a bishop lived at Garðar. In 1261 the Greenlanders accepted the overlordship of the Norwegian king, joining the Kingdom of Norway.
norse-greenland.e: The Western Settlement was abandoned in the mid-14th century, and the last written record from the Eastern Settlement is a wedding at Hvalsey church in 1408. By about 1450 the Norse had disappeared, probably owing to colder climate, falling ivory prices, isolation and emigration. Inuit, who had arrived from the 13th century, remained.

naxos.t: Largest island of the Cyclades, an Archaic marble-working power whose failed siege by Persia in 499 BCE set off the Ionian Revolt.
naxos.o: Naxos was settled by Ionian Greeks in the early Iron Age, building on a long Cycladic and Mycenaean past. Its fertile valleys and white marble made it the leading island of the Cyclades by the 7th century BCE. Tradition linked it with Dionysus and with Ariadne.
naxos.r: Naxian sculptors made colossal kouroi, the Naxian Sphinx at Delphi and the Lions on Delos. The tyrant Lygdamis, helped by Peisistratus, ruled in the mid-6th century BCE, when the great unfinished temple gateway, the Portara, was begun. In 499 BCE Aristagoras of Miletus and the Persians failed to capture Naxos, a fiasco that triggered the Ionian Revolt.
naxos.e: Persia sacked Naxos in 490 BCE. It was the first member to try to leave the Delian League and was subdued c. 470 BCE. Later it joined Hellenistic leagues and passed under Rome by 146 BCE.

numayrids.t: Arab emirs of the Banu Numayr who ruled Harran and the towns of the western Jazira for nearly a century.
numayrids.o: The Banu Numayr were a Bedouin tribe of the Amir ibn Sa'sa'a who moved into the Diyar Mudar, the region between the Euphrates and the Balikh. Around 990, as Hamdanid power faded, their chief Waththab ibn Sabiq seized Harran, and the tribe went on to hold Saruj, Raqqa and for a time Edessa.
numayrids.r: The Numayrids were tribal emirs who lived partly as nomads and relied on the townspeople and on dues from the fertile river valleys. They balanced between the Fatimids, the Mirdasids of Aleppo, the Marwanids and Byzantium. Harran still had a community of Sabian star-worshippers, whose temple the Numayrids are said to have turned into a palace. In 1031 they lost Edessa to Byzantine forces under George Maniakes.
numayrids.e: The Seljuk advance weakened the Bedouin emirates. Around 1081 the Uqaylid emir Muslim ibn Quraysh took Harran, ending Numayrid rule; the tribe itself survived in the region.

nagnatae.t: People of north-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, who also names a notable town of theirs called Nagnata.
nagnatae.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Nagnatae on the north-west coast of Ireland, roughly in Sligo or north Mayo, and lists a settlement called Nagnata, which he describes as a notable town. His information came from earlier sailors' reports on the Atlantic coast.
nagnatae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, economy or customs. The identification of Nagnata is disputed; sites around Sligo Bay have been suggested, and some versions of the text spell the people Magnatae, which has led to other proposed meanings. The region was rich in older monuments such as the Carrowmore tombs.
nagnatae.e: No later source mentions the Nagnatae. Their area later lay within the Kingdom of Connacht, ruled by branches of the Connachta dynasties.

nazca.t: A culture of Peru's southern desert famed for the Nazca Lines, giant figures and lines drawn on the desert floor, and for its brightly painted pottery.
nazca.o: The Nazca culture grew out of the late Paracas tradition around 100 BCE in the Río Grande de Nazca and Ica valleys of southern Peru. In its early phase the adobe ceremonial centre of Cahuachi, with dozens of mounds, served as a pilgrimage site for scattered farming communities.
nazca.r: Nazca appears to have been a group of chiefdoms linked by shared ritual rather than a centralised state. Its people created the Nazca Lines, hundreds of straight lines and figures of a monkey, hummingbird and spider scraped into the pampa, likely connected to water and fertility rites. They built underground aqueducts called puquios to tap groundwater. Their polychrome pottery used up to a dozen slip colours, and trophy heads feature prominently in their art.
nazca.e: Cahuachi lost importance by about 400 CE, and late Nazca society suffered from droughts and conflict. From around 650 CE the region came under the influence of the Wari Empire, and the Nazca style faded. The Lines became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.

najahid-dynasty.t: A dynasty of Ethiopian former slaves who ruled Zabid and the Yemeni Tihama for over a century amid wars with the Sulayhids.
najahid-dynasty.o: Najah was an Ethiopian slave commander serving the last rulers of the Ziyadid dynasty at Zabid. Around 1022 he took power for himself, gained recognition from the Abbasid caliph and founded a dynasty that ruled the Red Sea coastal plain of Yemen.
najahid-dynasty.r: The Najahids governed through Ethiopian slave troops and ministers, a pattern inherited from the Ziyadids, and supported Sunni scholarship in Zabid. Their history was dominated by war with the Isma'ili Sulayhid dynasty of the highlands: Najah was poisoned around 1060, and his son Sa'id al-Ahwal later killed the Sulayhid ruler Ali ibn Muhammad. Zabid changed hands several times, and in the 12th century viziers held real power.
najahid-dynasty.e: Weakened by internal rivalries, the dynasty fell to the Mahdid dynasty of Ali ibn Mahdi, who captured Zabid in 1159 after years of raids. The Ethiopian elite was largely destroyed.

nairi.t: Nairi, a loose confederation of highland chiefdoms around Lake Van that fought Assyria and became the seedbed of Urartu.
nairi.o: Nairi was the Assyrian name for the mountain lands north of the Tigris around Lake Van. After the Late Bronze Age collapse, local chiefdoms of the region formed temporary coalitions to resist Assyrian raids, first recorded by Tiglath-Pileser I c. 1100 BCE.
nairi.r: Tiglath-Pileser I claimed to have defeated 23 kings of Nairi and set up an inscription near Malazgirt. Nairi had no capital; it was a patchwork of fortified villages living from herding, farming and metalworking, which paid tribute in horses and cattle.
nairi.e: Repeated Assyrian campaigns under Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III pushed the Nairi chiefdoms to unite. By the mid-9th century BCE most were absorbed into the Kingdom of Urartu.

nuceria-alfaterna.t: Oscan city of southern Campania that led a league including Pompeii, Herculaneum and Stabiae before becoming an ally of Rome.
nuceria-alfaterna.o: Nuceria Alfaterna, modern Nocera Inferiore, grew in the Sarno valley inland from the Bay of Naples, on the route between Campania and the Gulf of Salerno. Its population was Oscan-speaking by the 5th century BCE, and earlier settlement shows Etruscan and Greek contacts.
nuceria-alfaterna.r: Nuceria headed a league of towns in the Sarno valley and along the coast, including Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae and Surrentum, and issued silver coins in Oscan with the name of the Alfaterni. It controlled a fertile plain producing grain, wine and fruit. Little else is known of its institutions.
nuceria-alfaterna.e: During the Second Samnite War Nuceria fought Rome but submitted in 308 BCE and became an ally on favourable terms. Hannibal destroyed it in 216 BCE for staying loyal to Rome, and it was later rebuilt. In 59 CE a riot between Nucerians and Pompeians in Pompeii's amphitheatre was recorded by Tacitus.

nesiotic-league.t: League of the Cycladic islands centred on Delos, created by Antigonus I and used by Hellenistic kings to control the Aegean.
nesiotic-league.o: Around 314 BCE Antigonus I Monophthalmus, seeking support in the Aegean against rival successors of Alexander, organised the islands of the Cyclades into a league with its headquarters at the sanctuary of Apollo on Delos. Members celebrated festivals named after Antigonus and his son Demetrius.
nesiotic-league.r: Delegates of the islands met in a federal council (synedrion) on Delos, voted honours for royal patrons and handled common affairs, but real power lay with the protecting king. After the collapse of Demetrius, the league passed under Ptolemaic control in the 280s BCE; officials called nesiarchs and Philocles, king of Sidon, acted for Ptolemy II, and the islanders founded the Ptolemaia festival.
nesiotic-league.e: Ptolemaic power in the Aegean waned in the mid-3rd century BCE and the league faded. It was revived around 200 BCE under Rhodian leadership, but ended in 167 BCE when Rome gave Delos to Athens and declared it a free port, ending Rhodian dominance.

nabataean-kingdom.t: The Nabataean Kingdom, an Arab trading state that controlled the incense routes and carved its capital Petra out of rose-red rock.
nabataean-kingdom.o: The Nabataeans were Arab nomads who controlled desert routes from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. By the 4th century BCE they were rich traders, and by 168 BCE they had a king, Aretas I, who appears in the Books of Maccabees. Petra, in the mountains of Edom, became their capital.
nabataean-kingdom.r: Nabataean kings ruled through control of the frankincense and myrrh trade, protected caravans and built cisterns and channels to store desert water. Petra's facades, such as Al-Khazneh, mix Greek, Egyptian and local styles. Aretas III held Damascus, and the Nabataean script developed into the Arabic alphabet.
nabataean-kingdom.e: The kingdom became a Roman client and declined as sea trade grew. When King Rabbel II died, Trajan annexed it in 106 CE as the province of Arabia Petraea.

nabhani-dynasty.t: A line of kings who ruled the Omani interior from Bahla for nearly five centuries between periods of Ibadi imamate.
nabhani-dynasty.o: The Banu Nabhan, an Arab tribe of the Azd, took power in inland Oman in the mid-12th century, as the Ibadi imamate weakened. Ruling as maliks, or kings, from Bahla and its great fort, they governed the interior while the coast was dominated by Hormuz.
nabhani-dynasty.r: Unlike elected Ibadi imams, the Nabhanis ruled by hereditary right, and Ibadi scholars often condemned them as tyrants. Their power waxed and waned; elected imams sometimes ruled alongside or instead of them from the 15th century. Their era is poorly documented, but the poet-king Sulayman ibn Sulayman al-Nabhani is remembered, and Bahla's walls and fort date largely from this period.
nabhani-dynasty.e: From the 16th century the Portuguese took the coast, including Portuguese Muscat. In 1624 Ibadi scholars elected Nasir ibn Murshid as imam, founding the Ya'aruba dynasty, which reunited Oman and ended Nabhani rule.

neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.t: A short-lived republic born of Masaniello's revolt against Spanish taxes in Naples, which briefly invited a French duke as its leader.
neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.o: In July 1647 a new tax on fruit sparked a rising in Naples led by the fisherman Tommaso Aniello, known as Masaniello. He was murdered within days, but the revolt spread, and in October 1647 the gunsmith Gennaro Annese proclaimed a republic independent of Spanish rule in the Kingdom of Naples.
neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.r: The rebels held most of the city while Spanish forces kept the castles and the fleet bombarded the town. They invited Henry II, Duke of Guise, a French claimant to the Angevin inheritance, who arrived in November and took the title Duke of the Republic. Quarrels between Guise, Annese and the nobles, and limited French support, weakened the regime, and the provinces were divided between rebels and barons.
neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.e: In April 1648, while Guise was outside the city, Spanish troops under Don John of Austria retook Naples with the help of Annese. Guise was captured, and Spanish rule was restored.

new-sweden.t: Sweden's short-lived colony on the Delaware River, which introduced the log cabin to North America before falling to the Dutch in 1655.
new-sweden.o: The New Sweden Company, with Dutch and Swedish investors, sent the ships Kalmar Nyckel and Fogel Grip under Peter Minuit, former director of New Netherland. In 1638 they bought land from the Lenape and built Fort Christina, at what is now Wilmington, Delaware, named after Queen Christina.
new-sweden.r: The colony never had more than a few hundred settlers, many of them Finns from the forests of Sweden and Finland, who brought the log cabin with them. Governor Johan Printz, in office from 1643 to 1653, ruled from Tinicum Island, built forts along the river and traded furs and tobacco with the Lenape and Susquehannock.
new-sweden.e: In 1654 Governor Johan Risingh seized the Dutch Fort Casimir, provoking a response. In 1655 Peter Stuyvesant of New Netherland arrived with ships and soldiers, and New Sweden surrendered. The settlers stayed and kept their Lutheran churches, such as Gloria Dei in Philadelphia, under Dutch and later English rule.

new-kingdom-of-granada.t: The Spanish colony created in Colombia's Andean highlands after the conquest of the Muisca, ruled from Santa Fe de Bogotá and the forerunner of Colombia.
new-kingdom-of-granada.o: Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada led an expedition up the Magdalena river and conquered the Muisca between 1537 and 1539. He founded Santa Fe de Bogotá in 1538 and named the land the New Kingdom of Granada after his home region in Spain. In 1549 a Royal Audiencia was established at Santa Fe.
new-kingdom-of-granada.r: From 1564 the territory was governed by a president of the Audiencia within the Viceroyalty of Peru. Its economy depended on gold from Antioquia, Popayán and the Chocó, mined increasingly by enslaved Africans, as well as emeralds from Muzo. Cartagena de Indias was the main port and a centre of the slave trade. The indigenous population fell sharply and was subject to encomienda and forced labour. The Jesuit Peter Claver ministered to enslaved Africans in Cartagena.
new-kingdom-of-granada.e: In 1717 the Spanish crown elevated the New Kingdom of Granada into the Viceroyalty of New Granada, separating it from Peru and adding Quito, Venezuela and Panama.

namnetes.t: Gallic people of the Loire estuary, allies of the Veneti against Caesar, who gave their name to the city of Nantes.
namnetes.o: The Namnetes lived on the north bank of the lower Loire, with a port called Condevicnum or Portus Namnetum on the site of Nantes. Strabo and Ptolemy place them between the Veneti and the Pictones, and Greek writers knew the Loire mouth as a trading point for Atlantic tin, linked to the earlier port of Corbilo.
namnetes.r: Little is known of their government. They took part in the Atlantic trade of the Armorican peoples and struck gold and silver coins of Armorican style.
namnetes.e: In 56 BCE the Namnetes sent help to the Veneti in their naval war against Caesar and shared in their defeat. Under Rome their port grew into the town of Condevicnum, renamed after the people as Namnetes, the origin of the name Nantes.

northern-march.t: A Saxon frontier march east of the Elbe, lost to the Slavs in 983 and revived as the territory that became the March of Brandenburg.
northern-march.o: When Margrave Gero died in 965 his huge march was split, and the northern part, between the Elbe and the Oder north of the Havel, became the Northern March. Its first margrave was Dietrich of Haldensleben, who ruled over the Hevelli and Lutician Slavs.
northern-march.r: The Northern March was a military frontier, defended by castles and supported by the bishoprics of Havelberg and Brandenburg. Dietrich's harsh rule helped provoke the Great Slav Rising of 983, after which German power collapsed east of the Elbe and the margraves held only the Altmark on the west bank, around Salzwedel and Stendal.
northern-march.e: In 1134 Lothair III granted the Northern March to the Ascanian Albert the Bear. After he secured Brandenburg in 1157, he took the title of Margrave of Brandenburg. The old march, with the Altmark as its western core, became part of the Margraviate of Brandenburg.
